question.prompt:
Values for \(A,\) \(B,\) \(C,\) and \(D\) are to be selected from \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) without replacement (i.e., no two letters have the same value). How many ways are there to make such choices so that the two curves \(y=Ax^2+B\) and \(y=Cx^2+D\) intersect?

(The order in which the curves are listed does not matter; for example, the choices \(A=3,\)\(B=2,\)\(C=4, \)\(D=1\) is considered the same as the choices \(A=4,\)\( B=1,\) \(C=3,\) \(D=2.\))

solutions.explanation:
At an intersection, \((A-C)x^2=D-B\). Since the four coefficients are distinct, neither side coefficient is zero. A real value of \(x\) exists precisely when \(A-C\) and \(D-B\) have the same sign: the narrower parabola must have the lower vertex.

The two curves are unordered, so name them uniquely by requiring \(A>C\). Then we must have \(B<D\). Choose the unordered pair \(\{A,C\}\) from six numbers in \(\binom62=15\) ways; its larger member is forced to be \(A\). Choose \(\{B,D\}\) from the four remaining numbers in \(\binom42=6\) ways; its smaller member is forced to be \(B\).

Every allowed pair of curves has exactly this one naming, so there is no further division by \(2\). The count is \(15\cdot6=\boxed{90}\), choice C. Giving an unordered object a unique order can prevent double counting.
solutions.title: Give the unordered parabola pair a unique naming and choose coefficient pairs.
